lesson.title: Shifting and Stretching: Linear Transformations of a Random Variable
lesson.summary: When a random variable is transformed by adding a constant and multiplying by another, its expected value shifts and scales along with it, but its variance responds only to the multiplication, never to the addition.
lesson.body:
Many real situations take an existing random variable X and convert it into a new variable using a linear rule of the form a plus b times X, where a and b are fixed numbers decided in advance. The constant a shifts every possible outcome up or down by the same fixed amount, the way a flat fee gets added on top of a variable charge. The constant b stretches or shrinks the outcomes, the way a price per unit scales with quantity.

Two rules describe exactly how this transformation affects expected value and variance, building directly on the last two chapters:

E(a + bX) = a + b times E(X)
Var(a + bX) = b squared times Var(X)

The reasoning behind these rules is worth understanding, not just memorizing. Adding the constant a shifts every possible outcome by the identical fixed amount, so the average shifts by that same amount too, but since every value moves together by the same distance, the values do not spread out or bunch up relative to each other at all, so the variance is completely unaffected by a. Multiplying by b, on the other hand, stretches or compresses the distances between values by a factor of b, so every deviation from the mean gets multiplied by b as well, and because variance involves squared deviations, the effect on variance is b squared rather than just b. Since standard deviation is the square root of variance, it follows that SD(a + bX) = the absolute value of b, times SD(X), using absolute value because a standard deviation itself can never be negative, even if b happens to be negative.

Continue with X, the number of pets in a randomly selected home, where E(X) = 1.3, Var(X) = 0.81, and SD(X) = 0.9 from earlier chapters. Suppose a pet sitting company charges a 10 dollar base fee for a home visit plus 15 dollars per pet in the home. The cost of a visit is a new random variable, Cost = 10 + 15X, so here a = 10 and b = 15.

Applying the expected value rule: E(Cost) = 10 + 15(1.3) = 10 + 19.5 = 29.5. The company earns 29.50 dollars per visit on average.

Applying the variance rule: Var(Cost) = 15 squared times Var(X) = 225 times 0.81 = 182.25. And SD(Cost) = 15 times SD(X) = 15 times 0.9 = 13.5, which matches the square root of 182.25 exactly, a useful consistency check.

It is tempting to think the 10 dollar base fee should also affect the variance, since it does appear in the Cost formula, but it does not. Every single visit gets exactly the same 10 dollars added, regardless of how many pets are there, so it shifts the average revenue upward but adds zero additional variability from visit to visit. Every bit of the variability in Cost comes from the variability in the number of pets, scaled up by the 15 dollar per pet rate.

Linear transformations of a single random variable are the building block for what comes next. Once you have two separate random variables and want to combine them by adding or subtracting them, the same underlying shift and scale logic reappears, but with one additional twist involving whether the two variables are independent.
